questions.stem: A laboratory plans to culture a newly received human respiratory isolate and use a procedure that may generate aerosols. What should be completed before selecting the containment level and equipment?
options: A protocol-specific risk assessment covering the agent, source, concentration, volume, aerosol potential, procedures, personnel, and facility capabilities.
Assign the highest biosafety level automatically because the specimen came from a person and the procedure may generate aerosols.
Begin the work in a standard open laboratory and increase controls only if employees report symptoms.
Select containment only from the organism name without considering the manipulation, volume, or aerosol generation.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Biosafety containment should be selected from the hazards of the agent and the work being performed. Protocol-driven risk assessment identifies the exposure routes and failure modes that the practices, safety equipment, and facility must control.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Using the highest level without assessing the agent and procedure can be impractical and does not replace a documented risk assessment.
Waiting for illness or exposure evidence is reactive and may allow preventable aerosol or contact exposure.
The same agent may require different controls depending on the procedure, scale, concentration, and likelihood of aerosol or splash generation.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); CDC/NIH Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories, 6th ed.
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 11, biological safety, containment, and biosafety levels, pp. 343-348; CDC/NIH BMBL 6th ed., principles of protocol-driven risk assessment

questions.stem: A responder finds blood mixed with another body fluid and cannot reliably determine the fluid type. Which approach is required for handling the material?
options: Handle it as ordinary waste in the facility unless the source person is known to have a diagnosed bloodborne infection.
Treat the material as potentially infectious and apply universal precautions, engineering and work-practice controls, and appropriate PPE.
Use gloves only and omit engineering or work-practice controls because PPE is the primary control.
Delay protective measures until laboratory testing confirms the presence of HIV, HBV, or HCV.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA requires universal precautions for blood and other potentially infectious materials. When body fluids cannot be differentiated, they are treated as potentially infectious rather than judged by appearance.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Universal precautions do not depend on a known diagnosis because infection status is often unknown.
Engineering and work-practice controls are required to eliminate or minimize exposure; PPE supplements them when exposure remains.
Protection is applied during the initial handling; testing does not replace immediate exposure controls.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 - Bloodborne Pathogens
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 11, biological exposure routes and containment, pp. 332-348; OSHA 1910.1030(d)(1)-(2)

questions.stem: A clinic has repeated needlestick injuries while staff recap conventional needles before disposal. Which corrective action best follows the bloodborne-pathogen control hierarchy?
options: Require thicker examination gloves while leaving the device and recapping process unchanged.
Post a detailed reminder, retrain staff to recap more carefully with two hands, and continue using the same conventional needles because the procedure is familiar and inexpensive.
Eliminate recapping where feasible, implement appropriate safety-engineered or needleless devices, place sharps containers at the point of use, and reinforce the revised work practice.
Move the sharps container to a locked central room so supervisors can monitor every disposal.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA gives priority to engineering and work-practice controls. Safety-engineered devices and accessible sharps containers reduce exposure at the source, while the work practice removes the recapping step that is producing injuries.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Ordinary gloves do not reliably prevent a puncture and do not correct the hazardous device or work practice.
A reminder alone does not address the recognized mechanism of injury or use available engineering controls.
Increasing the distance to disposal can increase handling and recapping and may create additional exposure opportunities.
questions.sourceTitle: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 - Bloodborne Pathogens; CDC/NIOSH - Bloodborne Infectious Disease Risk Factors and Post-Exposure Response
questions.sourceLocation: OSHA 1910.1030(d)(2), engineering and work-practice controls; CDC/NIOSH bloodborne disease prevention, safety-engineered sharps and disposal controls

questions.stem: A hospital adds a new procedure that changes which employees may contact blood and introduces a safer needle device. What should happen to the bloodborne-pathogen exposure control plan?
options: Wait for the next injury before revising the plan because the existing plan remains valid until an incident occurs.
Update only the PPE list and annual training slides because the exposure-control plan does not need to address engineering controls, task changes, employee input, or safer-device selection.
Replace the entire plan with the device manufacturer instructions and omit the exposure determination.
Review and update the plan to reflect the new tasks, positions, and engineering controls, including documented consideration of safer devices and input from affected non-managerial employees.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The exposure control plan is reviewed at least annually and whenever new or modified tasks, procedures, or positions affect occupational exposure. OSHA also requires consideration of safer devices and input from employees who use them.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The plan must be updated proactively when exposure conditions or controls change.
The plan includes methods of compliance, engineering controls, work practices, and the process for selecting safer devices.
Manufacturer instructions support device use but do not replace the employer-specific exposure determination and control program.
questions.sourceLocation: OSHA 1910.1030(c)(1), exposure control plan review and update; 1910.1030(c)(1)(iv)-(v), safer medical devices and employee input

questions.stem: An employee with occupational exposure initially signs the hepatitis B vaccination declination but requests the vaccine three months later while still performing exposed work. What is the employer expected to do?
options: Make the hepatitis B vaccination available at no cost after the employee changes the decision, provided occupational exposure continues.
Refuse the request because signing the declination permanently waives the vaccination benefit for the remainder of employment, even while occupational exposure continues.
Require the employee to pay because the initial employer offer was declined.
Wait until an exposure incident occurs before making vaccination available again.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: An employee may decline the vaccine initially and later accept it. OSHA requires the employer to make the vaccination available without cost to covered employees who remain occupationally exposed.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The declination is not permanent; the employee may later request vaccination.
The standard does not shift the cost to the employee after a later request while coverage continues.
Vaccination is preventive and should not be delayed until an exposure occurs.
questions.sourceLocation: OSHA 1910.1030(f)(1)-(2) and Appendix A, hepatitis B vaccination and declination

questions.stem: A technician receives a needlestick from a used hollow-bore needle. Which immediate response is most appropriate?
options: Squeeze the wound aggressively, scrub it with bleach, cover it tightly, and finish the shift before notifying a supervisor or seeking medical evaluation.
Wash the puncture with soap and water, report it immediately, and obtain prompt confidential medical evaluation and follow-up.
Cover the puncture and wait several days to see whether symptoms develop.
Report the incident only if the source person later tests positive for a bloodborne pathogen.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Immediate cleansing and prompt reporting allow rapid exposure assessment, documentation, source evaluation where permitted, and time-sensitive post-exposure management.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Caustic chemicals and aggressive manipulation are not recommended, and delay can interfere with timely medical management.
Bloodborne infections may be asymptomatic, and post-exposure evaluation is time sensitive.
The exposure should be reported and evaluated immediately even when source status is unknown.
questions.sourceTitle: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 - Bloodborne Pathogens; CDC/NIOSH - Bloodborne Infectious Disease Risk Factors and Post-Exposure Response
questions.sourceLocation: OSHA 1910.1030(f)(3), post-exposure evaluation and follow-up; CDC/NIOSH immediate response to sharps and mucous-membrane exposures

questions.stem: A worker has a positive TB blood test, no symptoms, a normal chest image, and negative sputum studies. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: Classify the worker as having active pulmonary tuberculosis and assume infectiousness solely from the positive blood test, despite the absence of symptoms and negative disease evaluation.
The positive blood test proves immunity and no follow-up is necessary.
The findings are consistent with inactive or latent TB infection; the worker is not contagious but should be evaluated for treatment to prevent progression.
The absence of symptoms proves the original test was false and should be ignored.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: People with inactive TB have viable but inactive organisms, usually test positive, have no symptoms, and cannot spread TB. Treatment reduces the risk of later active disease.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Active pulmonary disease requires evidence beyond a positive infection test; the described findings support inactive TB.
A positive infection test indicates infection, not immunity, and clinical evaluation and preventive treatment should be considered.
Inactive TB commonly produces no symptoms, so absence of symptoms does not invalidate the result.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); CDC - About Inactive Tuberculosis and About Tuberculosis
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 11, tuberculosis, pp. 334-335; CDC inactive TB characteristics and progression risk

questions.stem: A clinical laboratory performs routine manipulations of human blood specimens, including steps that can create splashes or aerosols. Which baseline approach is most defensible?
options: Use BSL-1 practices because the specimens are diagnostic rather than research materials.
Perform all work on an open bench as long as workers wear laboratory coats.
Use BSL-4 containment for every human blood specimen, regardless of the procedure, aerosol potential, specimen volume, or findings of the documented laboratory risk assessment.
Use BSL-2 practices and restricted access, apply bloodborne-pathogen controls, and perform aerosol- or splash-generating steps in a suitable biological safety cabinet.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Human blood may contain bloodborne pathogens. BSL-2 practices are commonly used for routine clinical specimens, while a biological safety cabinet provides primary containment for procedures likely to create aerosols or splashes.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Diagnostic purpose does not remove the potential for infectious agents in human specimens.
PPE alone does not adequately control procedures that may generate infectious aerosols or splashes.
BSL-4 is reserved for the highest-risk agents and is not the routine baseline for ordinary clinical blood handling.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); CDC/NIH Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories, 6th ed.; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 - Bloodborne Pathogens
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 11, BSL-2 and biological safety cabinets, pp. 344-347; CDC/NIH BMBL 6th ed., BSL-2 and clinical laboratory biosafety; OSHA 1910.1030

questions.concept: Class II biological safety cabinet function
questions.stem: Which statement best describes a properly used Class II biological safety cabinet during microbiological work?
options: It provides primary containment that protects personnel, the work, and the surrounding environment from biological aerosols through controlled airflow and HEPA filtration.
Treat it as a chemical fume hood intended for routine handling of volatile, flammable solvents while simultaneously performing open biological procedures that may generate aerosols.
It sterilizes every item placed inside, so surface decontamination and aseptic technique are unnecessary.
It protects only the sample and intentionally directs unfiltered air toward the worker.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A Class II cabinet is designed to protect the worker, product, and environment during suitable biological procedures. Correct placement, certification, airflow, and work technique are necessary for that protection.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A biological safety cabinet is not automatically suitable for chemical vapor control; chemical use depends on cabinet type and exhaust design.
The cabinet controls aerosols but does not automatically sterilize materials or replace proper technique and decontamination.
That description is inconsistent with personnel protection and controlled HEPA-filtered airflow.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); CDC/NIH Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories, 6th ed.
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 11, Class II biological safety cabinets, pp. 344-346; CDC/NIH BMBL 6th ed., primary containment equipment

questions.stem: A demolition crew must remove a large, dry accumulation of bat droppings from an enclosed attic in an area where Histoplasma may occur. Which plan best reduces worker exposure?
options: Dry sweep the material rapidly with several workers, keep the attic closed to prevent spread to adjacent rooms, and depend on short task duration instead of dust suppression or containment.

Restrict access, assess the task, suppress dust with appropriate wet methods, use controlled removal and containment, and select protective clothing and respiratory protection from the exposure assessment.
Use household odor masks because an absence of odor indicates that spores are not airborne.
Use compressed air to remove dust from rafters and rely on general room ventilation.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Disturbing bird or bat droppings can aerosolize Histoplasma spores. Preventing dust generation and using task-specific containment and PPE reduce inhalation and take-home exposure.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Dry sweeping can generate a high airborne spore concentration and spread contamination.
Histoplasma spores are not controlled or detected by odor, and ordinary nuisance masks may not provide suitable respiratory protection.
Compressed air disperses contaminated dust and can greatly increase aerosol exposure.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); CDC/NIOSH - Histoplasmosis and Work
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 11, histoplasmosis and biological containment, pp. 343-347; CDC/NIOSH histoplasmosis work-risk and dust-control guidance
